Our research compared the black hole mass of these radio-active galaxies to their star-forming activity in various regions, including both the central nucleus and the broader galaxy, with the aim of determining the contributing factor to this non-conformity. We used both spectroscopic and imaging data from the Optical Infrared Spectrograph Reconer (OIR) to carry out our analysis. Our results showed that for radio-active galaxies with a prominent active nucleus that fail to conform to the typical M*-SFR relation, the radio-active activity is concentrated in the central nucleus, leading to an underestimation of the black hole's mass based on star-forming activity in the broader galaxy. Consequently, this results in these galaxies appearing below the M*-SFR relation curve. This finding suggests that the radio-active activity in these galaxies is the primary cause of their non-conformity to the M*-SFR relation, rather than any other influencing factor.
